newsitem.title: UK: International LPG strongest in Europe on freeze.
newsitem.headline: International LPG strongest in Europe on freeze.

text.p: Europe remained the strongest market for LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) globally as the New Year brought continued freezing weather to much of the continent.
Propane is in demand across the continent as a domestic heating fuel, and prices are at their highest since the Gulf War as buyers scramble for supplies.
Trade reached a peak of $388 a tonne cif France early in the week, and many are convinced that prices will pass $400 and continue climbing while the cold persists.
And although the price differential between the U.S. and Europe makes arbitrage theoretically attractive, a shortage of vessels makes it unlikely that such movement will take place.

"The logistical problems are so big that it may not happen," said a Scandinavian trader. "There are not many ships, and there are loading problems as U.S. product is warm and needs to be cooled". He added that cooling propane to load on a refrigerated or semi-refrigerated vessel takes about seven days.

This means no product could arrive in Europe before the end of January at the earliest, and few traders are thought likely to risk importing product and face the possibility of a price collapse if the weather warms up.

And arrivals from the Middle East Gulf will also take time to arrive, dealers added, so at least in the short term Europe has become an isolated market where limited supply and rocketing demand are keeping prices very strong.

But large cargo trade in northern Europe has been hampered recently by the holiday season, and by the fact that BP, whose monthly Agreed Price or BPAP is the basis for much trade in north west Europe, has not yet published its January price. This is not now expected until Monday.

In the Mediterranean, propane is also strong, although prices have slipped since the beginning of the week, when a cargo traded at $396 a tonne cif Lavera. An Algerian trader explained that because of weather-related delays to trains carrying LPG to Italy, stocks are building up at Lavera and a lack of ullage is forcing prices down again.

And a Spanish trader confirmed that levels had slipped, saying that propane is now offered at $390 cif Lavera, although demand in Spain is still extremely strong. But he added that there are no serious uncovered requirements in Spain, and there will be no problem in meeting consumer demand.

Seagoing propane coasters are also extremely firm. One dealer pointed out that because inland demand, especially in the Rotterdam area, is so high, all available product is being drawn inland. "As a result there's not much available on the jetty," he said.
Seagoing coaster trade was concluded on Thursday at $395 a tonne fob UK East Coast, he added.
While buyers have kept propane strong in both northern Europe and the Mediterranean, the butane market has been quiet and prices have started to come down.
"There's some butane going into the heating market, but the numbers don't make sense for gasoline blending," said one barge trader.

In the Mediterranean, butane prices are purely notional, said dealers. The only way of assessing prices there is to look at official prices and add freight. On this basis, butane is notionally worth $340 a tonne cif Lavera, based on a Sonatrach price of $320 a tonne fob Bethioua and freight of $20 a tonne.
And in northwest Europe, a trader described the butane market as "dead quiet" and said that spot availabilities were moving to South America in the absence of local demand.

In the Far East, the market has been subdued as Golden Week in Japan has kept most players away from their desks. A trader assessed premiums over the Saudi CP at $40 to $45 a tonne basis Korea or Japan for both propane and butane, but added that requirements will not be known until traders return from holiday.

Chinese demand is also expected to pick up in the second half of the month with requirements for the Chinese New Year in February boosting demand, but there is no evidence of the demand yet, the trader added.

In the Middle East Gulf, spot cargoes are discussed at around CP +10 for propane and slightly higher for butane. India has taken a lot of butane recently, said a trader, and possible production problems meant that Saudi Aramco is being tight on tolerance, accounting for the higher value of butane than propane.
But eastern markets have been generally quiet, and the bulk of the interest and volatility remains firmly in Europe.
-- Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6412
